concepts.title: Circular Flow of Income
concepts.definition: The circular flow of income illustrates the continuous flow of goods, services and factor payments between firms and households in an economy.
concepts.key_idea: Production generates income, income generates expenditure, and expenditure generates production in a circular manner.
question_patterns: Define Circular Flow of Income and explain its components.
Distinguish between related terms in Introduction.
Compute Circular Flow of Income given numerical data.
Explain the significance of Circular Flow of Income in national income accounting.
Identify the correct formula and apply it to a problem on Circular Flow of Income.

solution_steps.explain: Households supply factors of production and consume goods; firms produce goods and use factors.
Real flow: factors and goods move. Money flow: factor payments and consumption expenditure move.
Total production equals total income equals total expenditure in a simple economy.

worked_examples.question: Explain the circular flow of income in a two-sector economy.
worked_examples.solution: Households supply factors to firms and receive factor incomes; firms supply goods to households and receive consumption expenditure.

worked_examples.question: Why is the circular flow called a continuous process?
worked_examples.solution: Each phase (production, income, expenditure) feeds the next, restarting the cycle.
worked_examples.answer: Because production, income and expenditure are mutually reinforcing and repeat continuously.

exercises.question: Draw and label the circular flow of income diagram.

concepts.title: GDP, GNP and NNP
concepts.definition: GDP is the market value of final goods and services produced within the domestic territory in a year. GNP is GDP plus net factor income from abroad. NNP is GNP minus depreciation.
concepts.formula: GNP = GDP + NFIA; NNP = GNP - Depreciation
concepts.key_idea: Domestic vs national aggregates differ by net factor income from abroad; gross vs net differ by depreciation.
question_patterns: Define GDP, GNP and NNP and explain its components.

concepts.title: Domestic vs National Income Aggregates
concepts.definition: Domestic aggregates measure income generated within the geographical territory; national aggregates include net factor income from abroad.
concepts.key_idea: The bridge between domestic and national aggregates is net factor income from abroad (NFIA).
question_patterns: Define Domestic vs National Income Aggregates and explain its components.
Distinguish between related terms in Basic Concepts.
Compute Domestic vs National Income Aggregates given numerical data.
Explain the significance of Domestic vs National Income Aggregates in national income accounting.
Identify the correct formula and apply it to a problem on Domestic vs National Income Aggregates.

solution_steps.explain: Start from the domestic measure (e.g. GDP).
NFIA = factor income earned by residents abroad minus factor income earned by non-residents domestically.
Add NFIA to the domestic aggregate to get the national aggregate.

worked_examples.question: Domestic income = Rs 20,000 crore, NFIA = Rs 1,000 crore. Find national income.

worked_examples.solution: Factor payments to the rest of the world exceed receipts from abroad.
worked_examples.answer: National income is less than domestic income.

concepts.title: Nominal GDP and Real GDP
concepts.definition: Nominal GDP is measured at current prices; real GDP is measured at constant base-year prices, removing the effect of price changes.
concepts.formula: Real GDP = Nominal GDP / GDP deflator x 100
concepts.key_idea: Real GDP reflects true changes in physical output by holding prices constant.
question_patterns: Define Nominal GDP and Real GDP and explain its components.
Distinguish between related terms in Real vs Nominal GDP.
Compute Nominal GDP and Real GDP given numerical data.
Explain the significance of Nominal GDP and Real GDP in national income accounting.
Identify the correct formula and apply it to a problem on Nominal GDP and Real GDP.

solution_steps.explain: Obtain GDP at current prices.
The deflator is the price index for GDP.
Deflate nominal GDP by the deflator.

worked_examples.question: Nominal GDP = Rs 12,000 crore, GDP deflator = 120. Find real GDP.
Why is real GDP a better measure of welfare than nominal GDP?
worked_examples.solution: Real GDP removes inflation, reflecting actual output changes.
worked_examples.answer: Real GDP captures real purchasing power and output growth.

concepts.title: GDP Deflator
concepts.definition: The GDP deflator is the ratio of nominal GDP to real GDP multiplied by 100; it measures the overall price level of all goods and services in GDP.
concepts.formula: GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) x 100
concepts.key_idea: The deflator reflects price changes between the current year and the base year.
question_patterns: Define GDP Deflator and explain its components.
Distinguish between related terms in Real vs Nominal GDP.
Compute GDP Deflator given numerical data.
Explain the significance of GDP Deflator in national income accounting.
Identify the correct formula and apply it to a problem on GDP Deflator.

solution_steps.explain: GDP at current prices.
GDP at base-year prices.

worked_examples.solution: Nominal GDP equals real GDP, so prices are at base-year levels.
worked_examples.answer: No price change relative to the base year.

concepts.title: Measurement of National Income: Value Added Method
concepts.definition: The value added method estimates national income by summing the value added by each producing unit in the economy.
concepts.formula: Value Added = Value of Output - Intermediate Consumption; GDP = sum of value added
concepts.key_idea: Value added avoids double counting by excluding the value of intermediate goods.
question_patterns: Define Measurement of National Income: Value Added Method and explain its components.
Distinguish between related terms in Measurement Methods.
Compute Measurement of National Income: Value Added Method given numerical data.
Explain the significance of Measurement of National Income: Value Added Method in national income accounting.
Identify the correct formula and apply it to a problem on Measurement of National Income: Value Added Method.

solution_steps.explain: Output quantity times price.
Deduct purchases of intermediate goods.
Add value added across all units to get GDP.

concepts.title: Measurement of National Income: Income Method
concepts.definition: The income method sums all factor incomes (wages, rent, interest and profit) paid to residents to estimate national income.
concepts.formula: NDPfc = Wages + Rent + Interest + Profit; NNPfc = NDPfc + NFIA
concepts.key_idea: National income is the sum of factor incomes earned by residents.
question_patterns: Define Measurement of National Income: Income Method and explain its components.

solution_steps.explain: Add compensation of employees, rent, interest and profit.
Add net factor income from abroad to convert domestic to national.
NNP at factor cost is national income.

concepts.title: Measurement of National Income: Expenditure Method
concepts.definition: The expenditure method estimates GDP by summing final consumption expenditure, investment expenditure and net exports.
concepts.key_idea: National income is obtained by aggregating final expenditures on goods and services.

concepts.title: GDP and Welfare
concepts.definition: GDP is often used as an indicator of welfare, but higher GDP does not always mean higher welfare due to distribution, composition and non-monetary factors.
concepts.key_idea: GDP growth is necessary but not sufficient for welfare improvement.
question_patterns: Define GDP and Welfare and explain its components.
Distinguish between related terms in GDP and Welfare.
Compute GDP and Welfare given numerical data.
Explain the significance of GDP and Welfare in national income accounting.
Identify the correct formula and apply it to a problem on GDP and Welfare.

solution_steps.explain: GDP measures market output, a common welfare proxy.
Distributional inequality, environmental costs and non-market activities are ignored.
GDP correlates with welfare but must be supplemented by other indicators.

worked_examples.question: Does a rise in GDP always imply a rise in welfare? Explain.
worked_examples.solution: Not necessarily; if inequality rises or environmental damage occurs, welfare may not improve.
worked_examples.answer: GDP is an imperfect but useful welfare indicator.

worked_examples.question: Name two limitations of GDP as a welfare measure.
worked_examples.solution: It ignores income distribution and non-market activities like housework.

exercises.question: Discuss the limitations of GDP as an indicator of welfare.
